AI optimizes diagnostics and treatments by analyzing
vast medical data, including Electronic Health Records
(EHRs) and image data, to identify patterns and accurately
predict outcomes. It aids in detecting diseases like cancer in
medical images, enhancing diagnoses and patient outcomes.
By analyzing medical history and genetic data, AI enables
early disease detection and suggests preventive measures,
improving patient care. Moreover, by automating routine
tasks, AI reduces healthcare costs and streamlines workﬂows,
allowing providers to focus on complex cases and improving
patient access to care [4].
However, some limitations must be considered. One of the
limitations is the inadequate diversity of the training data
utilized. For instance, if the training data consists of images
of breasts from only one ethnic group, it may not accurately
identify cancer in breasts from other ethnic groups [5].
Moreover, the systems might lack clarity, posing a challenge
for doctors to comprehend the reasoning guiding the system’s
decision-making process. This lack of transparency could be
troublesome in medical contexts, where human expertise and
intuition are necessary for accurate diagnosis [6], [7].
To address these limitations, Explainable Artiﬁcial Intelli-
gence (XAI) could be a promising approach that offers clear
explanations of AI systems’ decision-making processes. This
clarity increases trust in recommendations for both medical
professionals and patients, aiding informed decision-making.
Additionally, interpretability helps reduce false positives
and negatives, enhancing accuracy and minimizing risks in
diagnosis and treatment [8], [9], [10]. This article provides
a comprehensive overview of XAI techniques leveraged for
various state-of-the-art breast cancer detection applications.
Examples of these XAI techniques include case-based rea-
soning (CBR), visualization, and feature importance analysis.
Additionally, the emphasis is on the main XAI methods
discussed in the paper - LIME, SHAP, and GRAD CAM-
rather than focusing on others.
This article presents a systematic literature review (SLR)
examining the use of Explainable Artiﬁcial Intelligence
(XAI) strategies in breast-cancer detection and diagnosis.
We evaluate how XAI methods enhance model transparency
and trust in automated systems, identify prevailing gaps
across existing studies, highlight promising future paths for
XAI in medical imaging, and investigate the inﬂuence of XAI
on clinical decision-making and patient outcomes.
While prior reviews have focused on the broader appli-
cation of XAI in medical imaging, this paper narrows
the scope to breast-cancer diagnosis only. In doing so,
our contributions are three-fold: (a) We present a novel
mapping between explanation-methods, model types and bias
sources (i.e., a bias/explanation-method/model-type matrix).
(b) We conduct a quantitative meta-analysis of 44 selected
studies, assessing patterns of explanation-method usage
and model-explanation alignment. (c) We discussed about
evaluation frameworks that brings together bias detection and
fairness metrics, clinical workﬂow integration and usability
considerations for XAI in the breast-cancer context. These
S. Bai et al.: Breast Cancer Diagnosis With XAI: Uncovering Strengths and Biases
elements provide a focused and actionable overview that
goes beyond general XAI surveys and directly supports the
translation of XAI technologies into breast-cancer diagnostic
workﬂows.
The structure of the article is as follows: Section II
outlines the review methodology and protocol. Section III
presents the meta-analysis of selected studies, including
publication sources, citation trends, geographic distribution
and dataset modalities. Section IV provides an overview of
XAI techniques and analyzes their frequency of application
across various machine learning (ML) and deep learning
(DL) models. Section V discusses the speciﬁc XAI methods
utilized for explaining ML/DL models applied to primary
and secondary breast-cancer detection. Section VI offers a
comprehensive analysis of the most frequently employed
XAI techniques and their implications, while Section VII
concludes with a discussion of key implications and future
research directions.
II. REVIEW METHOD
This paper uses the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items on
Systematic Reviews and Meta-analysis) [11], [12] model.
As mentioned above, this SLR aims to identify and present
literature on XAI in breast cancer detection and diagnosis,
with a particular emphasis on their role in increasing
model transparency, thus enhancing trust in automated detec-
tion systems among healthcare professionals and patients.
This study will examine different XAI methods, including
model-agnostic and model-speciﬁc approaches, to assess
their ability to enhance breast cancer detection accuracy.
In summary, the objectives of this review are:
1) To identify, collect, and synthesize existing research on
the application of XAI techniques in the detection and
diagnosis of breast cancer.
2) To assess various XAI approaches, including both
model-agnostic and model-speciﬁc techniques, in terms
of their effectiveness in improving the transparency and
diagnostic accuracy of ML and DL models used for
breast cancer detection.
3) To explore the obstacles faced in integrating XAI
technologies into clinical workﬂows for breast cancer
diagnosis and to emphasize the importance of develop-
ing standardized metrics for evaluating the performance
and effectiveness of XAI models.
The study will also investigate how XAI techniques
can enhance trust in automated detection systems among
healthcare professionals and patients.
A. REVIEW PROTOCOL
This study was initiated by developing a thorough review
protocol aligned with established methodologies for com-
prehensive literature surveys [13]. The protocol serves as a
guide for the survey process by outlining key components
such as the study’s background, the literature search strategy,

overall quality of a selected group of studies. The following
criteria were applied to evaluate the quality of the chosen
studies.

the aims of this review article?
2) Does the research publication describe the approach and
methods clearly?
3) Is the data used in the study standardized? If not,

healthcare domain to predict and diagnose different diseases,
such as Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) [73], and other
kinds of cancer, for instance, lung cancer [74], breast
cancer [75], etc. However, the black-box aspect of these
models complicates interpretability, which is crucial for
clinical decision-making [76]. XAI approaches have been

A comprehensive taxonomy of XAI techniques is pre-

It is possible to explain and comprehend intrinsic models,
also called transparent models. Typical examples of trans-

and decision trees [112]. On the other hand, post-hoc is
categorized into model-speciﬁc and model-agnostic. XAI
explanations can also be categorized into two main types
based on their scope, which includes global and local.
A global explanation offers a comprehensive overview of
the entire model, while a local explanation focuses on a
single prediction or output. The speciﬁcs of various XAI

A. EVALUATION FRAMEWORKS AND METRICS FOR
EXPLAINABLE AI
XAI
seeks

requires a multifaceted approach that addresses both technical
rigor and user-centric considerations. A robust evaluation
framework ensures explanations are not only accurate and
reliable but also actionable and comprehensible to diverse
stakeholders.
Measuring
Explainable
Artiﬁcial
Intelligence
(XAI)
involves a multifaceted evaluation that balances technical
accuracy with user-centric effectiveness, ensuring explana-
tions are both reliable and actionable. Fidelity is a critical
metric, assessing how well explanations mirror the model’s
decision-making process. Methods such as Correlation
Metrics and Fidelity Scores, like Mean Squared Error (MSE),
compare explanations with model predictions to validate their
accuracy. Stability and Consistency are equally important,
as they measure whether explanations remain reliable under
slight input changes. This can be evaluated through Variance
Analysis and Consistency Scores, ensuring trust in the
system.
Another vital consideration is Computational Efﬁciency,
which focuses on the time and resources needed to generate
explanations. Tools like Runtime Analysis and Resource
Utilization are used to assess whether the system is
suitable for real-time or resource-constrained applications.
Beyond technical metrics, Comprehensibility and Usability
are central to the user experience. These are often measured
using User Surveys, Think-Aloud Protocols, and the System
Usability Scale (SUS) to gather feedback on the clarity,
coherence, and satisfaction users derive from explanations.

decisions. At the same time, Error Detection Rates and Bias

Grad-CAM (Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping)
[79] is a post-hoc technique that provides visual explanations
for the decisions made by convolutional neural networks
(CNNs). It achieves this by utilizing the gradients and feature
maps speciﬁc to a given CNN to highlight regions of an input
image that are most inﬂuential in the model’s prediction. This
reliance on the internal structure of CNNs, particularly the
gradients ﬂowing into the ﬁnal convolutional layers, makes
Grad-CAM a model-speciﬁc method tailored to convolu-
tional architectures. Consequently, it is not directly applicable
to non-convolutional models, such as those handling tabular
data. However, Grad-CAM is also model-agnostic in the
sense that it can be applied across various CNN architectures
without requiring modiﬁcations to each model’s speciﬁc
design. This ﬂexibility allows it to be used with a wide
range of CNN-based models, making it a versatile tool for
interpreting and visualizing CNN decisions [115].
The mathematical foundation of Grad-CAM is based on
the gradients of the target class with respect to the feature
maps. These gradients indicate the importance of each feature
map for the target prediction. Grad-CAM is particularly
useful for understanding and debugging CNNs in tasks such

answering.

D. LOCAL INTERPRETABLE MODEL-AGNOSTIC
EXPLANATIONS (LIME): MODEL-AGNOSTIC FRAMEWORK
FOR LOCAL EXPLAINABILITY
Ribeiro et al. [78] introduced LIME to explain predictions of
complex models like deep neural networks. LIME is a post-
hoc, model-agnostic technique that approximates the decision
boundary of a complex model as linear in the local vicinity of
the instance being explained. It generates perturbed samples
around the instance, obtains predictions from the complex
model, assigns weights based on proximity to the instance,
and builds an interpretable model on these weighted samples.
The goal is to provide a locally accurate and understandable
explanation for the instance in question, enhancing model
transparency.

been instrumental in clarifying the impact of key features,

algorithms like Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) to
improve the interpretability of survival predictions. Similarly,
Vrdoljak et al. [43] and Massafra et al. [45] employed
SHAP to interpret models predicting lymph node metastases,
demonstrating its effectiveness in making complex models
more comprehensible for clinical applications. Moreover,
SHAP has been used to compare traditional rule-based

E. SPECIALIZED XAI APPROACHES FOR BREAST CANCER
ANALYSIS
Beyond conventional explainable AI techniques, several
specialized approaches have been proposed to enhance inter-
pretability in breast cancer research, focusing on biomarker
analysis, automated tissue scoring, and hybrid image-based
models.
Idrees et al. [35] introduced XAI algorithms to analyze
potential biomarkers for breast cancer. Various classiﬁcation
models were applied to anthropometric data from three
studies [124], [125], [126], augmented with XAI models.
The results of these analyses revealed that serum levels of
HOMA, leptin, adiponectin, and resistin could
serve as novel biomarkers for breast cancer. The ﬁnd-
ings demonstrated sensitivity ranging from 83% to 87%,
speciﬁcity ranging from 81% to 88%, and AUC values
between 0.82 and 0.89 with a 95% conﬁdence interval. These
promising results suggest that integrating the characteristics
of HOMA, leptin, adiponectin, and resistin may
facilitate the development of a cost-effective breast cancer
biomarker.
Kabakcci et al. [26] proposed an automated method for
scoring CerbB2/HER2 receptors in breast cancer tissue
images, designed to replace the manual, error-prone scor-
ing traditionally performed by pathologists. This method
employs histogram-based analysis to separate tissue images
into color channels, segment cell nuclei and boundaries, and
extract features related to membrane staining intensity and
completeness. These extracted features are used to compute
cell-based HER2 scores, which are then aggregated to

VI. MAPPING EXPLAINABLE AI TO MACHINE LEARNING
AND DEEP LEARNING APPROACHES
This section explores the integration of XAI techniques
with various machine learning and deep learning models,
highlighting both their strengths and weaknesses. Addition-
ally, Table 5 provides valuable insights into the frequency
with which different machine learning and deep learning
models are paired with various explainability techniques. The
table also identiﬁes potential biases in certain deep learning
models, revealing a tendency to favor speciﬁc explainability
methods over others. This analysis aids in understanding the
limitations and advantages of different XAI techniques across
various contexts.
To begin with, SHAP is model-agnostic, meaning it is not
tied to any speciﬁc machine learning (ML) or deep learning
(DL) model. Refer to Figure 8 for a visualization created by
SHAP. This characteristic is advantageous because it allows
SHAP values to be applied to any machine learning model,
regardless of its architecture or underlying algorithms [128].
This ﬂexibility is particularly valuable for tasks involving
model comparison, as it provides a consistent method for
interpreting predictions and understanding model behavior.
Furthermore, because SHAP values are independent of the
speciﬁc model being used, they can be easily adapted
when the model is updated or replaced. In a machine
learning pipeline, where models are often reﬁned or replaced
over time, SHAP’s ﬂexibility ensures that the explanations
remain consistent and informative, requiring minimal effort
to integrate with updated models [129].
The Shapley values also offer three valuable properties not
found in other XAI methods [77], [131].
1) SHAP values provide local accuracy, meaning they
accurately capture the difference between the expected
output of the model and the output for a speciﬁc instance
of input data. This means they provide insights into how
individual features contribute to each prediction.
2) If a feature is missing (i.e. not present in the input data),
its attribution value in the SHAP analysis is set to zero,
ensuring that the absence of a feature is appropriately
accounted for in the explanation.
3) Changes in the model should not result in contradictory
changes to the SHAP values assigned to individual
features. If increasing the importance of a feature
model’s prediction also increases its corresponding
SHAP value, then consistency is maintained.
These properties make the SHAP model an ideal choice
for different rstudies’studies’ objectives. It offers a robust and
reliable method for explaining model predictions and com-
paring various models, regardless of their type or complexity.
For example, SHAP performed well with the XGBoost
model, as witnessed in [32], [41], [43], [45], and [48].
Despite its beneﬁts, the SHAP method may have
limitations.
1) The computational burden of computing SHAP values
can be signiﬁcant, potentially slowing down the analysis
process.
2) SHAP values are efﬁcient for tree-based models, for
example, XGBoost, but can be less effective for complex
architectures like deep learning models. The same can be
observed in Table 5.
In scenarios with limited computational resources or
when working with complex architectures such as deep
learning models, the application of SHAP is generally not
recommended.
Grad-CAM is one of the most widely used XAI methods
for medical imaging [132], as reﬂected in Table 5. It generates
heatmaps that highlight the regions of an image contributing
signiﬁcantly to the model’s decisions, offering insights into
the features or areas the model focuses on for classiﬁcation
(refer to Figure 8). This interpretability helps radiologists and
clinicians understand and validate the model’s predictions.
Grad-CAM’s ability to localize regions of interest in
medical images can assist in pinpointing abnormalities within
breast tissue, potentially improving diagnostic accuracy.
Studies such as [17], [18], [24], and [29] have demonstrated
that Grad-CAM is a valuable tool for corroborating the
ﬁndings of deep learning models by providing visual
evidence of the features driving their predictions.
However, like any other method, Grad-CAM also has
certain limitations:

Similar to SHAP, LIME is also model-agnostic, meaning

This local interpretability is particularly valuable in medical

However, while LIME explanations are locally faithful,
they may not always align with global model behavior,
as discussed in [42]. When applying LIME, researchers need

LIME’s explanations can be inconsistent across repeated

2) LIME lacks robustness as it provides a local approxima-

global behavior of the model.

A. EXPLAINABILITY FOR TRANSFORMER- AND
VISION-LANGUAGE CLINICAL AI
As clinical AI increasingly adopts Vision Transformers
(ViTs) and vision-language models (VLMs), evaluating
explainability requires more than visually plausible outputs.
Explanations must be decision-faithful, region-grounded,
robust, and fully auditable, ensuring that model rationales
can be rigorously veriﬁed and trusted. For ViTs, we advocate
transformer-aware pipelines that pair LRP-style relevance
propagation (to trace token→patch evidence) with attention
rollout/ﬂow (to characterize cross-layer information ﬂow),
and we insist that visualizations remain testable hypotheses.
Concretely: validate saliency with deletion/insertion curves
and sanity checks; run counterfactual/perturbation audits
(blur, mask, out-paint, or clinically plausible replacements) to
demonstrate necessity and sufﬁciency; and add concept-level
probes to estimate causal effects of named ﬁndings. These
steps directly address evidence that raw attention can mislead

B. OBSTACLES TO CLINICAL ADOPTION AND
STANDARDISED EVALUATION OF XAI IN BREAST CANCER
DIAGNOSIS
Despite the substantial promise of explainable artiﬁcial
intelligence (XAI) in breast cancer diagnostics, signiﬁcant
challenges persist on the path from research prototypes to
routine clinical implementation. A key challenge is the lack
of standardised evaluation frameworks: while many studies
report model accuracy, far fewer assess how well explanations
support human decision-making, inter-operator consistency,
or workﬂow integration. Reviews of XAI evaluation methods
in healthcare highlight that many papers rely on anecdotal
evidence or bespoke user studies, and only a minority
adopt shared frameworks, thereby limiting cross study
comparability and trust in explanation outputs [148], [149],
[150]. In the speciﬁc domain of breast-cancer diagnosis, this
evaluation gap undermines study comparability, reduces clin-
ician conﬁdence in explanation tools, and limits replicability
of results.
Another major barrier is the limited real-world valida-
tion and generalisability of current XAI systems. Many
breast-cancer detection studies rely on retrospective or single
centre datasets with homogeneous populations or imaging
devices, raising questions about external validity across
breast densities, ethnic groups, or device vendors [151],
[152]. Without thorough multi centre validation and diverse
cohorts, even technically advanced XAI tools may fail when
transferred to real-world clinical settings.
Third, there is an inherent trade-off between explainability,
accuracy and bias. Complex deep-learning models (such as
convolutional neural networks) may yield high diagnostic
performance but require post-hoc explanation tools whose
ﬁdelity is not always guaranteed; conversely, simpler models
may be interpretable but less robust. Many tree-based models
are paired with SHAP/LIME, while CNN-based image
models often rely on saliency maps reﬂecting a bias in
model-explanation matching that our survey also revealed.
Furthermore, if training data lacks diversity, explanation
methods may systematically emphasise features pertinent in
one domain but not in others, thereby embedding fairness
risks [153].
Even when explanations are generated, the interpretability
and usability of those explanations for end-users (clinicians,
pathologists) remain under-explored. For example, a heat-
map produced by Grad-CAM may appear intuitive, yet
unless validated to correspond to a clinically-relevant patho-
logical landmark, the clinician may ignore or mistrust it.
Human-centred evaluation studies show wide variation in
clinician comprehension and trust of different explanation
formats, emphasising the need for user centric design and
training [149].
Finally, workﬂow integration, ethical and regulatory issues
present additional hurdles. Deploying an XAI enabled system
in radiology or pathology services requires alignment with
existing PACS/EHR systems, audit trails, clinician account-
ability and clear responsibility when AI recommendations
(and explanations) are delivered. Reviews of AI in screening
note that regulatory, ethical and governance frameworks
are still emergent and must evolve to support XAI-enabled
clinical care [154], [155]. The deployment of such AI
systems raises questions about liability, informed consent,
transparency, and data-fairness especially in high-stakes
domains such as breast-cancer diagnosis.
In light of these gaps, recent literature suggests several
strategic directions:
• Develop and adopt clinically-oriented, standardised
evaluation metrics and benchmark frameworks for XAI
in breast-cancer diagnostics. The literature strongly
emphasises

• Expand multi centre, multi-modality and population-

• Design human-in-the-loop, workﬂow-embedded eval-

• Tailor explanation methods to match the user group

C. BRIDGING BIAS DISCOVERY TO CLINICAL IMPACT AND
MITIGATION
Beyond identifying methodological and data-centric biases,
it is crucial to understand how these biases manifest in clinical
workﬂows. For instance, spurious correlations in imaging
datasets such as scanner artefacts, skin markers or acquisition
metadata inadvertently correlated with malignancy labels
can lead XAI models to focus on non-pathological cues.
Clinically, such biases may distort malignancy estimation
and inﬂuence biopsy decisions, thereby impacting patient
safety and diagnostic conﬁdence. Recent work emphasises
that bias is a systemic concern at every stage of AI for
medical imaging, from data sampling to deployment, making
proactive detection and correction essential [158]. Moreover,
frameworks like the ‘‘Reveal to Revise’’ life-cycle explicitly
combine explanation-based bias identiﬁcation with model
revision and re-evaluation, demonstrating how counterfactual
testing, feature sensitivity analysis or domain-adversarial
methods can attenuate spurious dependencies [159]. Embed-
ding such mitigation mechanisms into model development
and explanation evaluation therefore closes the translational
loop from bias discovery to clinical practice, improving
diagnostic robustness and enhancing clinician trust in XAI
systems. Future work should extend these strategies through
clinician-in-the-loop bias audits and post-deployment mon-

itoring to ensure sustained fairness and reliability across
diverse patient populations.
To support the translation of XAI into breast-cancer
diagnostics, we propose an evaluation framework (shown in
Figure 9 composed of four inter-linked domains:
• Technical & Fidelity: Assess how well explanations
mirror the model’s internal reasoning (e.g., ﬁdelity,
stability, runtime) and whether explanation methods
reveal model errors or biases.
• Fairness & Bias-Detection: Quantify and mitigate bias
sources (e.g., dataset imbalance, device shift, spurious
correlations), evaluate cross-population robustness, and
measure fairness of explanations across sub-groups.
• Usability & Clinician Trust: Capture human centred
metrics of how easily clinicians understand and act on
explanations (e.g., usability scales, think-aloud proto-
cols, decision-error reduction, trust/conﬁdence metrics).
• Workﬂow & Clinical Integration: Evaluate how the
XAI system embeds into real-world clinical workﬂows:
interoperability with PACS/EHR, audit-trail readi-
ness, clinician AI collaboration, and regulatory/ethical
readiness.
If these pathways are followed, the transition of XAI from
promising research prototypes into trustworthy clinical tools
for breast cancer diagnosis becomes far more likely.
VII. CONCLUSION
XAI plays a crucial role in evaluating model performance,
which is essential for optimizing accuracy and reliability in
practical applications. Beyond performance, it is imperative
to assess the impact of XAI on user trust and comprehension.
As AI technologies become increasingly integrated into
healthcare, ensuring their transparency and interpretability

treatment decisions, which is particularly important in com-
plex cases like breast cancer, where patient-speciﬁc factors
signiﬁcantly inﬂuence outcomes. In addition to technical
advancements, addressing the ethical implications of using
AI in breast cancer diagnosis is imperative. The deployment
of AI models in clinical settings must be guided by rigorous
ethical standards to ensure patient privacy, data security,
and equitable access to healthcare beneﬁts. Transparency
in AI decision-making, achieved through XAI techniques,
not only enhances trust among healthcare professionals
and patients but also mitigates biases that may stem from

ABSTRACT Breast cancer is one of the most common malignancies afﬂicting women globally, necessitating
the use of cutting-edge AI approaches in diagnostic procedures to improve patient outcomes drastically.
However, one key difﬁculty with the most recent AI models is a lack of transparency, making it difﬁcult for
medical practitioners to implement these technologies to increase diagnostic accuracy. Many explainable
AI (XAI) solutions have been developed to overcome this issue. This survey focuses on applying XAI
approaches in breast cancer detection and diagnosis, particularly emphasizing their role in increasing model
transparency and clinical decision-making. The article also provides insights into the inherent biases in
the most recent machine learning models towards speciﬁc XAI approaches, such as the compatibility of
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) with visual explanation methods and tree-based models with feature
signiﬁcance evaluations. Finally, the article covers the obstacles to using XAI technologies in clinical practice
and the signiﬁcance of deﬁning standard measures for assessing their performance.
INDEX TERMS
Explainable artiﬁcial intelligence (XAI), breast cancer detection, interpretability,
transparency, medical imaging, clinical decision-making.
I. INTRODUCTION

Breast cancer is categorized into three primary groups
that reﬂect the stage of the disease and the complexity of
treatment. Primary breast cancer, which makes up 80% of
cases, is found initially in the breast without having spread
beyond the breast or the lymph nodes under the arms.
Secondary breast cancer, constituting 14% of cases, involves
cancer spreading to other parts of the body, such as the lungs,
bones, or liver. The smallest group, which accounts for 6%
of cases, includes those with both primary and secondary
characteristics due to recurrence, indicating that the cancer
has returned after treatment, either at the original site or
elsewhere. The studies reviewed in this article are distributed
according to the abovementioned categories.
Breast cancer (BC) ranks as the predominant form of cancer
in adults worldwide, with an alarming rate of over 2.3 million
new cases each year, as reported by the World Health
Organization (WHO) 2022 [1]. Breast cancer survival rates
vary signiﬁcantly across the globe, with a majority of deaths
occurring in low- and middle-income countries. Early detec-
tion is crucial as it leads to a clinical cure rate of over 90%,
but this decreases signiﬁcantly as the cancer progresses [2].
Integrating artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) techniques into breast
cancer diagnosis can improve early diagnosis and patient
outcomes. AI systems’ ability to analyze large datasets,
recognize patterns, and perform predictive analysis can

AI optimizes diagnostics and treatments by analyzing
vast medical data, including Electronic Health Records
(EHRs) and image data, to identify patterns and accurately
predict outcomes. It aids in detecting diseases like cancer in
medical images, enhancing diagnoses and patient outcomes.
By analyzing medical history and genetic data, AI enables
early disease detection and suggests preventive measures,
improving patient care. Moreover, by automating routine
tasks, AI reduces healthcare costs and streamlines workﬂows,
allowing providers to focus on complex cases and improving
patient access to care [4].
However, some limitations must be considered. One of the
limitations is the inadequate diversity of the training data
utilized. For instance, if the training data consists of images
of breasts from only one ethnic group, it may not accurately
identify cancer in breasts from other ethnic groups [5].
Moreover, the systems might lack clarity, posing a challenge
for doctors to comprehend the reasoning guiding the system’s
decision-making process. This lack of transparency could be
troublesome in medical contexts, where human expertise and
intuition are necessary for accurate diagnosis [6], [7].
To address these limitations, Explainable Artiﬁcial Intelli-
gence (XAI) could be a promising approach that offers clear
explanations of AI systems’ decision-making processes. This
clarity increases trust in recommendations for both medical
professionals and patients, aiding informed decision-making.
Additionally, interpretability helps reduce false positives
and negatives, enhancing accuracy and minimizing risks in
diagnosis and treatment [8], [9], [10]. This article provides
a comprehensive overview of XAI techniques leveraged for
various state-of-the-art breast cancer detection applications.
Examples of these XAI techniques include case-based rea-
soning (CBR), visualization, and feature importance analysis.
Additionally, the emphasis is on the main XAI methods
discussed in the paper - LIME, SHAP, and GRAD CAM-
rather than focusing on others.
This article presents a systematic literature review (SLR)
examining the use of Explainable Artiﬁcial Intelligence
(XAI) strategies in breast-cancer detection and diagnosis.
We evaluate how XAI methods enhance model transparency
and trust in automated systems, identify prevailing gaps
across existing studies, highlight promising future paths for
XAI in medical imaging, and investigate the inﬂuence of XAI
on clinical decision-making and patient outcomes.
While prior reviews have focused on the broader appli-
cation of XAI in medical imaging, this paper narrows
the scope to breast-cancer diagnosis only. In doing so,
our contributions are three-fold: (a) We present a novel
mapping between explanation-methods, model types and bias
sources (i.e., a bias/explanation-method/model-type matrix).
(b) We conduct a quantitative meta-analysis of 44 selected
studies, assessing patterns of explanation-method usage
and model-explanation alignment. (c) We discussed about
evaluation frameworks that brings together bias detection and
fairness metrics, clinical workﬂow integration and usability
considerations for XAI in the breast-cancer context. These
S. Bai et al.: Breast Cancer Diagnosis With XAI: Uncovering Strengths and Biases
elements provide a focused and actionable overview that
goes beyond general XAI surveys and directly supports the
translation of XAI technologies into breast-cancer diagnostic
workﬂows.
The structure of the article is as follows: Section II
outlines the review methodology and protocol. Section III
presents the meta-analysis of selected studies, including
publication sources, citation trends, geographic distribution
and dataset modalities. Section IV provides an overview of
XAI techniques and analyzes their frequency of application
across various machine learning (ML) and deep learning
(DL) models. Section V discusses the speciﬁc XAI methods
utilized for explaining ML/DL models applied to primary
and secondary breast-cancer detection. Section VI offers a
comprehensive analysis of the most frequently employed
XAI techniques and their implications, while Section VII
concludes with a discussion of key implications and future
research directions.
II. REVIEW METHOD
This paper uses the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items on
Systematic Reviews and Meta-analysis) [11], [12] model.
As mentioned above, this SLR aims to identify and present
literature on XAI in breast cancer detection and diagnosis,
with a particular emphasis on their role in increasing
model transparency, thus enhancing trust in automated detec-
tion systems among healthcare professionals and patients.
This study will examine different XAI methods, including
model-agnostic and model-speciﬁc approaches, to assess
their ability to enhance breast cancer detection accuracy.
In summary, the objectives of this review are:
1) To identify, collect, and synthesize existing research on
the application of XAI techniques in the detection and
diagnosis of breast cancer.
2) To assess various XAI approaches, including both
model-agnostic and model-speciﬁc techniques, in terms
of their effectiveness in improving the transparency and
diagnostic accuracy of ML and DL models used for
breast cancer detection.
3) To explore the obstacles faced in integrating XAI
technologies into clinical workﬂows for breast cancer
diagnosis and to emphasize the importance of develop-
ing standardized metrics for evaluating the performance
and effectiveness of XAI models.
The study will also investigate how XAI techniques
can enhance trust in automated detection systems among
healthcare professionals and patients.
A. REVIEW PROTOCOL
This study was initiated by developing a thorough review
protocol aligned with established methodologies for com-
prehensive literature surveys [13]. The protocol serves as a
guide for the survey process by outlining key components
such as the study’s background, the literature search strategy,

The review protocol separates SLRs from traditional or
narrative literature reviews. It improves the uniformity of the
review process. It reduces researcher bias by demanding the
provision of an explicit search strategy as well as established
criteria for the inclusion and removal of studies.
B. CRITERIA FOR INCLUSION AND EXCLUSION
Setting precise inclusion and exclusion criteria guarantees
that only pertinent articles on breast cancer diagnosis using
XAI are included in this study. We focused on studies
published in reputable journals from January 2019 to June
2025. Our initial search based on the listed keywords resulted
in 6302 research articles (refer to Figure 1 for a complete
overview of the selection process). After a thorough review
of the articles, we excluded articles that were unrelated to an
XAI but appeared in the search because of keyword match.
Additionally, articles were also excluded based on duplicity
and non-availability of full text.
C. SEARCH STRATEGY
To conduct this survey, our search strategy aimed to gather
relevant research articles addressing the application of XAI
in breast cancer detection. Both automatic and manual search
methods were employed to ensure comprehensive coverage
of the available literature.
The automatic search was conducted using reputable
databases known for hosting scholarly works related to XAI
and healthcare, refer to Figure 1. These databases were
selected for their extensive collection of relevant research
articles in the ﬁeld. While other sources such as magazines,
working papers, newspapers, books, and blogs contain
valuable information, they were not included in this survey
due to the lack of rigorous peer-review processes, which
could potentially compromise the reliability and quality of
the ﬁndings.
A variety of general keywords exploring different aspects
of XAI in breast cancer diagnosis were used for the search.
These keywords were derived from the research questions

using User Surveys, Think-Aloud Protocols, and the System
Usability Scale (SUS) to gather feedback on the clarity,
coherence, and satisfaction users derive from explanations.

1) GRAD-CAM
Grad-CAM (Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping)
[79] is a post-hoc technique that provides visual explanations
for the decisions made by convolutional neural networks
(CNNs). It achieves this by utilizing the gradients and feature
maps speciﬁc to a given CNN to highlight regions of an input
image that are most inﬂuential in the model’s prediction. This
reliance on the internal structure of CNNs, particularly the
gradients ﬂowing into the ﬁnal convolutional layers, makes
Grad-CAM a model-speciﬁc method tailored to convolu-
tional architectures. Consequently, it is not directly applicable
to non-convolutional models, such as those handling tabular
data. However, Grad-CAM is also model-agnostic in the
sense that it can be applied across various CNN architectures
without requiring modiﬁcations to each model’s speciﬁc
design. This ﬂexibility allows it to be used with a wide
range of CNN-based models, making it a versatile tool for
interpreting and visualizing CNN decisions [115].
The mathematical foundation of Grad-CAM is based on
the gradients of the target class with respect to the feature
maps. These gradients indicate the importance of each feature
map for the target prediction. Grad-CAM is particularly
useful for understanding and debugging CNNs in tasks such

EXPLANATIONS (LIME): MODEL-AGNOSTIC FRAMEWORK

Ribeiro et al. [78] introduced LIME to explain predictions of
complex models like deep neural networks. LIME is a post-
hoc, model-agnostic technique that approximates the decision
boundary of a complex model as linear in the local vicinity of
the instance being explained. It generates perturbed samples
around the instance, obtains predictions from the complex
model, assigns weights based on proximity to the instance,
and builds an interpretable model on these weighted samples.
The goal is to provide a locally accurate and understandable
explanation for the instance in question, enhancing model
transparency.

VI. MAPPING EXPLAINABLE AI TO MACHINE LEARNING
AND DEEP LEARNING APPROACHES
This section explores the integration of XAI techniques
with various machine learning and deep learning models,
highlighting both their strengths and weaknesses. Addition-

with which different machine learning and deep learning
models are paired with various explainability techniques. The
table also identiﬁes potential biases in certain deep learning
models, revealing a tendency to favor speciﬁc explainability
methods over others. This analysis aids in understanding the
limitations and advantages of different XAI techniques across
various contexts.
To begin with, SHAP is model-agnostic, meaning it is not
tied to any speciﬁc machine learning (ML) or deep learning
(DL) model. Refer to Figure 8 for a visualization created by
SHAP. This characteristic is advantageous because it allows
SHAP values to be applied to any machine learning model,
regardless of its architecture or underlying algorithms [128].
This ﬂexibility is particularly valuable for tasks involving
model comparison, as it provides a consistent method for
interpreting predictions and understanding model behavior.
Furthermore, because SHAP values are independent of the
speciﬁc model being used, they can be easily adapted
when the model is updated or replaced. In a machine
learning pipeline, where models are often reﬁned or replaced
over time, SHAP’s ﬂexibility ensures that the explanations
remain consistent and informative, requiring minimal effort
to integrate with updated models [129].
The Shapley values also offer three valuable properties not
found in other XAI methods [77], [131].
1) SHAP values provide local accuracy, meaning they
accurately capture the difference between the expected
output of the model and the output for a speciﬁc instance
of input data. This means they provide insights into how
individual features contribute to each prediction.
2) If a feature is missing (i.e. not present in the input data),
its attribution value in the SHAP analysis is set to zero,
ensuring that the absence of a feature is appropriately
accounted for in the explanation.
3) Changes in the model should not result in contradictory
changes to the SHAP values assigned to individual
features. If increasing the importance of a feature
model’s prediction also increases its corresponding
SHAP value, then consistency is maintained.
These properties make the SHAP model an ideal choice
for different rstudies’studies’ objectives. It offers a robust and
reliable method for explaining model predictions and com-
paring various models, regardless of their type or complexity.
For example, SHAP performed well with the XGBoost
model, as witnessed in [32], [41], [43], [45], and [48].
Despite its beneﬁts, the SHAP method may have
limitations.
1) The computational burden of computing SHAP values
can be signiﬁcant, potentially slowing down the analysis
process.
2) SHAP values are efﬁcient for tree-based models, for
example, XGBoost, but can be less effective for complex
architectures like deep learning models. The same can be
observed in Table 5.
In scenarios with limited computational resources or
when working with complex architectures such as deep
learning models, the application of SHAP is generally not
recommended.
Grad-CAM is one of the most widely used XAI methods
for medical imaging [132], as reﬂected in Table 5. It generates
heatmaps that highlight the regions of an image contributing
signiﬁcantly to the model’s decisions, offering insights into
the features or areas the model focuses on for classiﬁcation
(refer to Figure 8). This interpretability helps radiologists and
clinicians understand and validate the model’s predictions.
Grad-CAM’s ability to localize regions of interest in
medical images can assist in pinpointing abnormalities within
breast tissue, potentially improving diagnostic accuracy.
Studies such as [17], [18], [24], and [29] have demonstrated
that Grad-CAM is a valuable tool for corroborating the
ﬁndings of deep learning models by providing visual
evidence of the features driving their predictions.
However, like any other method, Grad-CAM also has
certain limitations:

A. EXPLAINABILITY FOR TRANSFORMER- AND
VISION-LANGUAGE CLINICAL AI
As clinical AI increasingly adopts Vision Transformers
(ViTs) and vision-language models (VLMs), evaluating
explainability requires more than visually plausible outputs.
Explanations must be decision-faithful, region-grounded,
robust, and fully auditable, ensuring that model rationales
can be rigorously veriﬁed and trusted. For ViTs, we advocate
transformer-aware pipelines that pair LRP-style relevance
propagation (to trace token→patch evidence) with attention
rollout/ﬂow (to characterize cross-layer information ﬂow),
and we insist that visualizations remain testable hypotheses.
Concretely: validate saliency with deletion/insertion curves
and sanity checks; run counterfactual/perturbation audits
(blur, mask, out-paint, or clinically plausible replacements) to
demonstrate necessity and sufﬁciency; and add concept-level
probes to estimate causal effects of named ﬁndings. These
steps directly address evidence that raw attention can mislead

B. OBSTACLES TO CLINICAL ADOPTION AND
STANDARDISED EVALUATION OF XAI IN BREAST CANCER
DIAGNOSIS
Despite the substantial promise of explainable artiﬁcial
intelligence (XAI) in breast cancer diagnostics, signiﬁcant
challenges persist on the path from research prototypes to
routine clinical implementation. A key challenge is the lack
of standardised evaluation frameworks: while many studies
report model accuracy, far fewer assess how well explanations
support human decision-making, inter-operator consistency,
or workﬂow integration. Reviews of XAI evaluation methods
in healthcare highlight that many papers rely on anecdotal
evidence or bespoke user studies, and only a minority
adopt shared frameworks, thereby limiting cross study
comparability and trust in explanation outputs [148], [149],
[150]. In the speciﬁc domain of breast-cancer diagnosis, this
evaluation gap undermines study comparability, reduces clin-
ician conﬁdence in explanation tools, and limits replicability
of results.
Another major barrier is the limited real-world valida-
tion and generalisability of current XAI systems. Many
breast-cancer detection studies rely on retrospective or single
centre datasets with homogeneous populations or imaging
devices, raising questions about external validity across
breast densities, ethnic groups, or device vendors [151],
[152]. Without thorough multi centre validation and diverse
cohorts, even technically advanced XAI tools may fail when
transferred to real-world clinical settings.
Third, there is an inherent trade-off between explainability,
accuracy and bias. Complex deep-learning models (such as
convolutional neural networks) may yield high diagnostic
performance but require post-hoc explanation tools whose
ﬁdelity is not always guaranteed; conversely, simpler models
may be interpretable but less robust. Many tree-based models
are paired with SHAP/LIME, while CNN-based image
models often rely on saliency maps reﬂecting a bias in
model-explanation matching that our survey also revealed.
Furthermore, if training data lacks diversity, explanation
methods may systematically emphasise features pertinent in
one domain but not in others, thereby embedding fairness
risks [153].
Even when explanations are generated, the interpretability
and usability of those explanations for end-users (clinicians,
pathologists) remain under-explored. For example, a heat-
map produced by Grad-CAM may appear intuitive, yet
unless validated to correspond to a clinically-relevant patho-
logical landmark, the clinician may ignore or mistrust it.
Human-centred evaluation studies show wide variation in
clinician comprehension and trust of different explanation
formats, emphasising the need for user centric design and
training [149].
Finally, workﬂow integration, ethical and regulatory issues
present additional hurdles. Deploying an XAI enabled system
in radiology or pathology services requires alignment with
existing PACS/EHR systems, audit trails, clinician account-
ability and clear responsibility when AI recommendations
(and explanations) are delivered. Reviews of AI in screening
note that regulatory, ethical and governance frameworks
are still emergent and must evolve to support XAI-enabled
clinical care [154], [155]. The deployment of such AI
systems raises questions about liability, informed consent,
transparency, and data-fairness especially in high-stakes
domains such as breast-cancer diagnosis.
In light of these gaps, recent literature suggests several
strategic directions:
• Develop and adopt clinically-oriented, standardised
evaluation metrics and benchmark frameworks for XAI
in breast-cancer diagnostics. The literature strongly
emphasises
that
without
such
metrics—covering
ﬁdelity, stability, usability and domain relevance XAI
explanations cannot be reliably compared or trusted
across studies [148].
• Expand multi centre, multi-modality and population-
diverse validation studies to establish generalisability
and fairness. Many XAI systems to date rely on single
centre or homogeneous datasets; broad validation is
required to ensure robustness across devices, modalities
and patient populations [153].
• Design human-in-the-loop, workﬂow-embedded eval-
uations, where clinicians interact with the AI + XAI
system and their decision-making, trust and outcomes
are formally measured. Human AI collaboration is
now identiﬁed as a key element of trustworthy
implementation [156].
• Tailor explanation methods to match the user group
(radiologist, pathologist, oncologist) and the model type
(tree-based, CNN, multimodal). Explanation formats
that are technically accurate but misaligned to the

• Address bias, fairness, ethics and regulatory readiness

Without careful attention to fairness of explanations, lia-

C. BRIDGING BIAS DISCOVERY TO CLINICAL IMPACT AND
MITIGATION
Beyond identifying methodological and data-centric biases,
it is crucial to understand how these biases manifest in clinical
workﬂows. For instance, spurious correlations in imaging
datasets such as scanner artefacts, skin markers or acquisition
metadata inadvertently correlated with malignancy labels
can lead XAI models to focus on non-pathological cues.
Clinically, such biases may distort malignancy estimation
and inﬂuence biopsy decisions, thereby impacting patient
safety and diagnostic conﬁdence. Recent work emphasises
that bias is a systemic concern at every stage of AI for
medical imaging, from data sampling to deployment, making
proactive detection and correction essential [158]. Moreover,
frameworks like the ‘‘Reveal to Revise’’ life-cycle explicitly
combine explanation-based bias identiﬁcation with model
revision and re-evaluation, demonstrating how counterfactual
testing, feature sensitivity analysis or domain-adversarial
methods can attenuate spurious dependencies [159]. Embed-
ding such mitigation mechanisms into model development
and explanation evaluation therefore closes the translational
loop from bias discovery to clinical practice, improving
diagnostic robustness and enhancing clinician trust in XAI
systems. Future work should extend these strategies through
clinician-in-the-loop bias audits and post-deployment mon-

itoring to ensure sustained fairness and reliability across
diverse patient populations.
To support the translation of XAI into breast-cancer
diagnostics, we propose an evaluation framework (shown in
Figure 9 composed of four inter-linked domains:
• Technical & Fidelity: Assess how well explanations
mirror the model’s internal reasoning (e.g., ﬁdelity,
stability, runtime) and whether explanation methods
reveal model errors or biases.
• Fairness & Bias-Detection: Quantify and mitigate bias
sources (e.g., dataset imbalance, device shift, spurious
correlations), evaluate cross-population robustness, and
measure fairness of explanations across sub-groups.
• Usability & Clinician Trust: Capture human centred
metrics of how easily clinicians understand and act on
explanations (e.g., usability scales, think-aloud proto-
cols, decision-error reduction, trust/conﬁdence metrics).
• Workﬂow & Clinical Integration: Evaluate how the
XAI system embeds into real-world clinical workﬂows:
interoperability with PACS/EHR, audit-trail readi-
ness, clinician AI collaboration, and regulatory/ethical
readiness.
If these pathways are followed, the transition of XAI from
promising research prototypes into trustworthy clinical tools
for breast cancer diagnosis becomes far more likely.
VII. CONCLUSION
XAI plays a crucial role in evaluating model performance,
which is essential for optimizing accuracy and reliability in
practical applications. Beyond performance, it is imperative
to assess the impact of XAI on user trust and comprehension.
As AI technologies become increasingly integrated into
healthcare, ensuring their transparency and interpretability

is vital for fostering trust among medical practitioners
and patients. Integrating various XAI approaches, however,
presents signiﬁcant challenges, particularly in comparative
analysis and generalization across diverse scenarios. This
complexity highlights the need for a robust framework
to evaluate these models comprehensively. Establishing
standardized evaluation metrics is critical, as they provide
consistent and reliable measures of effectiveness in clinical
settings. These metrics should not only assess the accuracy
and efﬁciency of XAI applications but also evaluate the
quality of the explanations in terms of relevance, complete-
ness, and consistency. Moreover, the integration of XAI
into clinical workﬂows can advance personalized medicine.
By offering tailored explanations, XAI can help clinicians
understand the reasoning behind speciﬁc diagnostic or
treatment decisions, which is particularly important in com-
plex cases like breast cancer, where patient-speciﬁc factors
signiﬁcantly inﬂuence outcomes. In addition to technical
advancements, addressing the ethical implications of using
AI in breast cancer diagnosis is imperative. The deployment
of AI models in clinical settings must be guided by rigorous
ethical standards to ensure patient privacy, data security,
and equitable access to healthcare beneﬁts. Transparency
in AI decision-making, achieved through XAI techniques,
not only enhances trust among healthcare professionals
and patients but also mitigates biases that may stem from
non-representative training data.
